study.title: Jeremiah 47 The judgment on the Philistines and the sword that does not hold
study.overview: Jeremiah 47 announces judgment against the Philistines, the historical enemies of Israel, by means of an image of flooding from the north and a sword that executes the judgment of the Lord. The chapter shows that God rules the nations, directs the time of events, and uses human instruments to fulfill their righteousness. At the same time, the text describes the complete collapse of human trust: cities in lament, parents without the strength to help their children, and a useless attempt to make the sword "parar" before fulfilling their mission.

outline.title: The word against the Philistines and the North Flood
outline.explanation: The chapter begins by placing the prophecy against the Philistines before the Egyptian attack on Gaza. Then the Lord describes the enemy advance as overflowing waters that come from the north, a figure for the invasion that drags cities and peoples to panic.

outline.title: The terror of war and ruin of the Philistine cities
outline.explanation: The bang of the cars, horses and wheels produces fear so great that parents lose their strength to act. The text then exposes the devastation of Gaza and Ascalom, using mourning and total cut images of the territory, showing a widespread and humiliating destruction.

outline.title: The sword of the Lord cannot be interrupted
outline.explanation: The final scene presents the sword as if it had its own voice. The request for her to return to the sheath receives as an answer that she cannot rest, because she received order from the Lord against Ascalom and the sea coast. The judgment advances until completing its mission.

study.context: The chapter addresses the Philistines, a people sitting on the Mediterranean coastline, the recurring enemy of Israel. The notes provided relate the prophecy to the action of Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian invasion, seen as the means used by God to judge these cities. The text also mentions Gaza, Ascalom, Tyre and Sidom, which reinforces the scenario of disturbance in the coastal region.
study.theology: Jeremiah 47 teaches that the Lord is not a spectator of history, but the judge of the nations. He determines both the event and his time, and even hostile forces of the war function under his commission. The image of the waters of the north communicates the irresistibility of the divine judgment when its moment comes. The personification of the sword at the end of the chapter highlights that violence is not released to chance; it remains under superior authority. At the same time, the passage denounces the uselessness of resisting the divine decree when sin matured for judgment. In evangelical reading, the text also calls reverence before the holiness of God and repentance before judgment is completed.

scholarViews.insight: The "undundation" depicts the advance of the Babylonian armies over the coastal strip, showing that the devastation of the Philistines was linked to the invasion of Babylon and the time set by God.
The chapter shows the fate of the Philistines by the same hand that judged other peoples; war would be long, and attempts to make it cease would be useless.
The sword of the Lord is presented as an agent of judgment: she received commission against Ascalom and the sea coast, so that she cannot rest before fulfilling her task.

questions: What does the image of the flood teach about the speed and strength of God's judgment when it arrives?
How does the description of the fear and weakness of parents reveal human insufficiency in the face of divine discipline?
How does the chapter correct the idea that world history is given only to chance or to political power?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to abandon any confidence in human power, territorial advantage or political security as if they were absolute. The concrete application is to cultivate a reverent fear before God, to quickly confess sin and not to harden the heart when the Lord warns. It is also worth examining whether, instead of fighting against divine correction, one is submitting to God's government with repentance, humility, and obedience.
